title: Chapter 7: Memory — Making AI Assistants Remember Context
content:
Chapter 7: Memory — Making AI Assistants Remember Context

Opening Hook: The Difference Between a Chatbot and a Helpful Assistant

A chatbot answers what you ask right now.

A useful assistant remembers what matters.

Imagine asking:

Explain RAG.

A normal chatbot gives a general explanation.

But a memory-powered assistant can answer differently if it remembers:

The user is a beginner Python learner. The user prefers short examples. The user is building a portfolio project. The user is interested in freelancing.

Now the answer can be more helpful:

RAG is a way to let your Python AI app answer using your own documents. For your portfolio, you could build a PDF chatbot that retrieves relevant chunks before answering.

That is the value of memory.

Memory helps an AI assistant become more personal, more useful, and more consistent.

But memory also creates risk.

If an assistant remembers everything, it may store secrets, private data, or sensitive information the user never wanted saved.

So the goal is not:

Remember everything.

The goal is:

Remember useful, user-approved information safely.

In this chapter, you will build a personal study or work assistant with memory.

It will let the user explicitly save memories with a /remember command, view saved memories, delete memories, clear memory, and use memory as context in future responses.

This chapter teaches one of the most important design rules for practical AI agents:

Memory should be useful, visible, editable, and user-controlled.

What You Will Learn

By the end of this chapter, you will understand:

  • What memory means in AI assistants
  • The difference between short-term and long-term memory
  • Why memory improves personalization
  • Why memory creates privacy risks
  • How to store user-approved memory locally
  • How to inspect and delete memory
  • How to include memory in prompts safely
  • How to block obvious secrets from being saved
  • How to build a personal study or work assistant with memory
  • How to test memory logic without live API calls
  • How memory connects to future workflow and capstone projects

Why This Chapter Matters

In earlier chapters, your assistant could answer, summarize, retrieve, search, and use tools.

But each request was mostly isolated.

A memory-powered assistant can carry useful context across interactions.

For example:

User: /remember I am preparing for Python interviews. Later: Explain decorators.

The assistant can now respond with interview preparation in mind.

Another example:

User: /remember I prefer concise bullet-point explanations. Later: Explain vector databases.

The assistant can keep the answer short and structured.

Memory is powerful because it improves relevance.

But memory must be handled carefully.

A poorly designed memory system can:

  • Store secrets
  • Store private information
  • Remember incorrect facts
  • Use irrelevant memory
  • Expose one user’s information to another user
  • Make the assistant feel creepy
  • Make deletion difficult

This chapter uses the safest beginner pattern:

The assistant remembers only when the user explicitly says /remember. The user can inspect memory. The user can delete memory. The user can clear all memory.

That is simple, practical, and respectful.

7.1 What Is Memory in an AI Assistant?

Memory is stored information that the assistant can use later.

In a Python AI app, memory might be stored in:

  • A JSON file
  • A SQLite database
  • A vector database
  • A cloud database
  • A user profile table
  • A conversation history store

For this chapter, you will use a local JSON file.

That keeps the project beginner-friendly.

A memory item might look like this:

{ "id": 1, "text": "The user prefers concise explanations.", "tags": ["preference"], "created_at": "2026-05-23T10:30:00" }

When the user asks a question, the assistant can include relevant memory in the prompt.

7.2 Short-Term Memory vs Long-Term Memory

There are two common types of memory.

Short-Term Memory

Short-term memory usually means recent conversation context.

Example:

User: I am building a PDF chatbot. Assistant: Great. User: How should I test it?

The assistant understands that “it” means the PDF chatbot.

Short-term memory is often stored only during the current session.

Long-Term Memory

Long-term memory persists across sessions.

Example:

The user is building Python AI portfolio projects. The user prefers beginner-friendly explanations. The user is interested in freelancing.

Long-term memory can be useful, but it must be controlled carefully.

This chapter focuses on simple long-term memory saved to a JSON file.

7.3 What Should an Assistant Remember?

Good memory examples:

The user prefers concise answers. The user is learning Python. The user is building a RAG app. The user wants portfolio project advice. The user prefers examples using simple code.

Bad memory examples:

The user's API key is sk-... The user's password is ... The user's private token is ... The user's bank details are ... The user's private medical information is ...

Do not store secrets.

Do not store sensitive information unless your app has a real privacy design and the user clearly understands what is being stored.

For beginner projects, keep memory simple and low-risk.

7.4 User-Controlled Memory

A safe beginner memory system should support:

/remember [text] /memory /forget [id] /clear_memory

This gives the user control.

The assistant should not silently save everything.

Silent memory can feel invasive.

Explicit memory feels respectful.

The user says what should be remembered.

The user can review it.

The user can delete it.

That is the design you will build.

7.5 Project: Personal Study or Work Assistant with Memory

What This Project Does

This project builds a command-line assistant with memory.

It supports:

/ask [question] /remember [memory] /memory /forget [id] /clear_memory /help /exit

Examples:

/remember I prefer concise bullet-point explanations. /ask Explain RAG. /memory /forget 1

The assistant uses saved memory as context when answering questions.

Who This Helps

This project helps:

  • Students
  • Python learners
  • Developers
  • Freelancers
  • Professionals
  • Productivity tool builders
  • Anyone building more personal AI assistants

What You Will Build

Create this project structure:

chapter_07_memory_assistant/ .env.example .gitignore requirements.txt llm_client.py memory_store.py prompts.py commands.py assistant.py app.py test_memory_store.py test_commands.py test_assistant.py README.md

7.6 Setup

Step 1: Create the Folder

mkdir chapter_07_memory_assistant cd chapter_07_memory_assistant

Step 2: Create a Virtual Environment

python -m venv .venv

Activate it.

On macOS or Linux:

source .venv/bin/activate

On Windows PowerShell:

.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1

Step 3: Create requirements.txt

openai python-dotenv pytest

Install dependencies:

pip install -r requirements.txt

Step 4: Create .env.example

OPENAI_API_KEY=replace_with_your_api_key OPENAI_MODEL=gpt-4.1-mini OPENAI_TEMPERATURE=0.2 MEMORY_FILE=memory.json

Copy it to .env.

On macOS or Linux:

cp .env.example .env

On Windows PowerShell:

Copy-Item .env.example .env

Then edit .env and add your real API key.

Never publish your real .env file.

7.7 File: .gitignore

Create .gitignore:

.env .venv/ __pycache__/ .pytest_cache/ *.pyc *.log memory.json

The memory file may contain user preferences or private notes, so do not commit it.

7.8 File: llm_client.py

Create llm_client.py:

""" Chapter 7: Reusable LLM Client """ import os from dataclasses import dataclass, field from dotenv import load_dotenv from openai import OpenAI load_dotenv() def get_env_float(name: str, default: float) -> float: """Read a float from environment variables safely.""" raw_value = os.getenv(name) if raw_value is None: return default try: return float(raw_value) except ValueError: return default @dataclass class LLMConfig: """Configuration for the LLM client.""" model: str = field( default_factory=lambda: os.getenv("OPENAI_MODEL", "gpt-4.1-mini") ) temperature: float = field( default_factory=lambda: get_env_float("OPENAI_TEMPERATURE", 0.2) ) class LLMClient: """Small reusable client for sending prompts to an LLM.""" def __init__(self, config: LLMConfig | None = None): self.config = config or LLMConfig() api_key = os.getenv("OPENAI_API_KEY") if not api_key: raise ValueError( "OPENAI_API_KEY is missing. Add it to your .env file." ) self.client = OpenAI(api_key=api_key) def complete(self, system: str, user: str) -> str: """Send a request to the model and return text output.""" if not system.strip(): raise ValueError("System instruction cannot be empty.") if not user.strip(): raise ValueError("User request cannot be empty.") model_input = f""" System instruction: {system.strip()} User request: {user.strip()} """ response = self.client.responses.create( model=self.config.model, input=model_input, temperature=self.config.temperature, ) return response.output_text class MockLLMClient: """Mock client for tests.""" def __init__(self, response_text: str = "Mock response"): self.response_text = response_text self.calls: list[dict[str, str]] = [] def complete(self, system: str, user: str) -> str: """Return fixed output and record the call.""" if not system.strip(): raise ValueError("System instruction cannot be empty.") if not user.strip(): raise ValueError("User request cannot be empty.") self.calls.append( { "system": system, "user": user, } ) return self.response_text Not executed automatically: requires live API credentials, network access, or external service.

7.9 File: memory_store.py

This file stores and manages memory.

Create memory_store.py:

""" Local JSON memory store for the Chapter 7 memory assistant. This beginner-friendly memory store supports: - Add memory - List memory - Delete memory by ID - Clear all memory Do not store secrets, passwords, API keys, or sensitive private data. """ import json import os import re from dataclasses import dataclass, asdict from datetime import datetime from pathlib import Path from dotenv import load_dotenv load_dotenv() def get_memory_path() -> Path: """Return the configured memory file path.""" return Path(os.getenv("MEMORY_FILE", "memory.json")) @dataclass class MemoryItem: """One saved memory item.""" id: int text: str created_at: str def default_memory_data() -> dict: """Return default memory file structure.""" return { "next_id": 1, "items": [], } SECRET_PATTERNS = [ r"sk-[A-Za-z0-9_\-]{10,}", r"api[_-]?key\s*[:=]\s*[A-Za-z0-9_\-]{10,}", r"password\s*[:=]\s*\S+", r"token\s*[:=]\s*[A-Za-z0-9_\-\.]{10,}", ] def looks_like_secret(text: str) -> bool: """ Basic heuristic for detecting possible secrets. This is not a complete secret scanner, but it catches common beginner mistakes. """ lowered = text.lower() secret_keywords = [ "api key", "password", "private key", "secret key", "access token", "bearer token", ] if any(keyword in lowered for keyword in secret_keywords): return True return any(re.search(pattern, text, re.IGNORECASE) for pattern in SECRET_PATTERNS) def load_memory_data(path: Path | None = None) -> dict: """Load memory data from JSON.""" memory_path = path or get_memory_path() if not memory_path.exists(): return default_memory_data() try: data = json.loads(memory_path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")) except json.JSONDecodeError: return default_memory_data() if not isinstance(data, dict): return default_memory_data() if "next_id" not in data or "items" not in data: return default_memory_data() return data def save_memory_data(data: dict, path: Path | None = None) -> None: """Save memory data to JSON.""" memory_path = path or get_memory_path() memory_path.write_text(json.dumps(data, indent=2), encoding="utf-8") def add_memory(text: str, path: Path | None = None) -> MemoryItem: """Add a memory item.""" cleaned = text.strip() if not cleaned: raise ValueError("Memory cannot be empty.") if len(cleaned) > 500: raise ValueError("Memory is too long. Limit: 500 characters.") if looks_like_secret(cleaned): raise ValueError( "This memory appears to contain a secret or sensitive credential. " "Do not store API keys, passwords, or tokens." ) data = load_memory_data(path) memory_id = int(data["next_id"]) item = MemoryItem( id=memory_id, text=cleaned, created_at=datetime.now().isoformat(timespec="seconds"), ) data["items"].append(asdict(item)) data["next_id"] = memory_id + 1 save_memory_data(data, path) return item def list_memory(path: Path | None = None) -> list[MemoryItem]: """List all saved memories.""" data = load_memory_data(path) items = [] for raw_item in data.get("items", []): try: items.append( MemoryItem( id=int(raw_item["id"]), text=str(raw_item["text"]), created_at=str(raw_item["created_at"]), ) ) except (KeyError, TypeError, ValueError): continue return items def delete_memory(memory_id: int, path: Path | None = None) -> bool: """Delete memory by ID. Return True if deleted.""" data = load_memory_data(path) original_count = len(data["items"]) data["items"] = [ item for item in data["items"] if int(item.get("id", -1)) != memory_id ] deleted = len(data["items"]) < original_count if deleted: save_memory_data(data, path) return deleted def clear_memory(path: Path | None = None) -> None: """Clear all memory.""" save_memory_data(default_memory_data(), path) def format_memory_for_display(path: Path | None = None) -> str: """Format memory for terminal display.""" items = list_memory(path) if not items: return "No saved memory." lines = [] for item in items: lines.append(f"{item.id}. {item.text}") lines.append(f" saved: {item.created_at}") return "\n".join(lines) def format_memory_for_prompt(path: Path | None = None) -> str: """Format memory for inclusion in an LLM prompt.""" items = list_memory(path) if not items: return "No saved memory." lines = [] for item in items: lines.append(f"- {item.text}") return "\n".join(lines) Test result: Python syntax check passed.

7.10 File: prompts.py

Create prompts.py:

""" Prompt templates for the Chapter 7 memory assistant. """ MEMORY_ASSISTANT_SYSTEM_PROMPT = """ You are a helpful personal study and work assistant. You may receive saved memory about the user's preferences, goals, or context. Rules: - Use saved memory only when it is relevant. - Do not mention memory unnecessarily. - Do not invent facts about the user. - Do not reveal sensitive information. - Be clear, practical, and encouraging. - If memory conflicts with the current request, prioritize the current request. """ def build_memory_prompt(user_request: str, memory_context: str) -> str: """Build prompt that includes saved memory.""" return f""" Saved memory: {memory_context} Current user request: {user_request} Respond helpfully. If the saved memory is relevant, use it to personalize the answer. If the saved memory is not relevant, ignore it. Do not claim to remember anything that is not listed in saved memory. """ Test result: Python syntax check passed.

7.11 File: commands.py

Create commands.py:

""" Command parsing for the Chapter 7 memory assistant. """ from dataclasses import dataclass SUPPORTED_COMMANDS = { "/help", "/ask", "/remember", "/memory", "/forget", "/clear_memory", "/exit", } @dataclass class ParsedCommand: """A parsed command.""" command: str content: str def parse_command(user_input: str) -> ParsedCommand: """Parse user input into command and content.""" cleaned = user_input.strip() if not cleaned: return ParsedCommand(command="", content="") if not cleaned.startswith("/"): return ParsedCommand(command="/ask", content=cleaned) parts = cleaned.split(maxsplit=1) command = parts[0].lower() content = parts[1].strip() if len(parts) > 1 else "" return ParsedCommand(command=command, content=content) def is_supported_command(command: str) -> bool: """Return True if command is supported.""" return command in SUPPORTED_COMMANDS def help_text() -> str: """Return help text.""" return """ Available commands: /ask [question] Ask the assistant a question using saved memory when relevant. /remember [memory] Save a user-approved memory. Example: /remember I prefer concise bullet-point explanations. /memory Show saved memory. /forget [id] Delete one memory by ID. Example: /forget 2 /clear_memory Delete all saved memory. /help Show this help message. /exit Quit the assistant. Privacy note: Do not save API keys, passwords, tokens, or sensitive private data. """.strip() Test result: Python syntax check passed.

7.12 File: assistant.py

Create assistant.py:

""" Assistant logic for the Chapter 7 memory assistant. """ from commands import parse_command, is_supported_command, help_text from llm_client import LLMClient, MockLLMClient from memory_store import ( add_memory, list_memory, delete_memory, clear_memory, format_memory_for_display, format_memory_for_prompt, ) from prompts import MEMORY_ASSISTANT_SYSTEM_PROMPT, build_memory_prompt def handle_remember(content: str) -> str: """Handle /remember command.""" if not content.strip(): return "Please provide something to remember." try: item = add_memory(content) return f"Saved memory {item.id}: {item.text}" except ValueError as error: return f"Memory not saved: {error}" def handle_forget(content: str) -> str: """Handle /forget command.""" if not content.strip(): return "Please provide the memory ID to delete. Example: /forget 2" try: memory_id = int(content.strip()) except ValueError: return "Memory ID must be a number." deleted = delete_memory(memory_id) if deleted: return f"Deleted memory {memory_id}." return f"No memory found with ID {memory_id}." def handle_ask(content: str, client=None) -> str: """Handle /ask command.""" if not content.strip(): return "Please enter a question." llm = client or LLMClient() memory_context = format_memory_for_prompt() prompt = build_memory_prompt( user_request=content, memory_context=memory_context, ) return llm.complete( system=MEMORY_ASSISTANT_SYSTEM_PROMPT, user=prompt, ) def handle_command(user_input: str, client=None) -> str: """ Handle one command and return a response. """ parsed = parse_command(user_input) if not parsed.command: return "Please enter a command or question." if parsed.command == "/exit": return "EXIT" if parsed.command == "/help": return help_text() if not is_supported_command(parsed.command): return f"Unknown command: {parsed.command}\nType /help to see available commands." if parsed.command == "/remember": return handle_remember(parsed.content) if parsed.command == "/memory": return format_memory_for_display() if parsed.command == "/forget": return handle_forget(parsed.content) if parsed.command == "/clear_memory": clear_memory() return "All memory cleared." if parsed.command == "/ask": return handle_ask(parsed.content, client=client) return "Command was recognized but not handled." Test result: Python syntax check passed.

7.13 File: app.py

Create app.py:

""" Chapter 7 Project: Personal Study or Work Assistant with Memory """ from assistant import handle_command def print_welcome() -> None: """Print welcome text.""" print("\nPersonal Study or Work Assistant with Memory") print("=" * 60) print("Type /help to see commands.") print("Type /remember to save user-approved memory.") print("Type /exit to quit.") print("=" * 60) def main() -> None: """Run the memory assistant.""" print_welcome() while True: try: user_input = input("\nYou: ").strip() response = handle_command(user_input) if response == "EXIT": print("\nAssistant: Goodbye.") break print("\nAssistant:") print(response) except KeyboardInterrupt: print("\n\nAssistant: Goodbye.") break except Exception as error: print("\nAssistant:") print(f"Something went wrong: {error}") if __name__ == "__main__": main() Test result: Python syntax check passed.

7.14 File: test_memory_store.py

Create test_memory_store.py:

from pathlib import Path import pytest from memory_store import ( add_memory, list_memory, delete_memory, clear_memory, format_memory_for_display, format_memory_for_prompt, looks_like_secret, ) def test_add_memory(tmp_path: Path): memory_file = tmp_path / "memory.json" item = add_memory("I prefer concise answers.", memory_file) assert item.id == 1 assert item.text == "I prefer concise answers." items = list_memory(memory_file) assert len(items) == 1 def test_add_memory_rejects_empty(tmp_path: Path): memory_file = tmp_path / "memory.json" with pytest.raises(ValueError): add_memory(" ", memory_file) def test_add_memory_rejects_secret(tmp_path: Path): memory_file = tmp_path / "memory.json" with pytest.raises(ValueError): add_memory("My API key is abcdefghijklmnop", memory_file) def test_looks_like_secret(): assert looks_like_secret("password=abc123") is True assert looks_like_secret("I like short explanations.") is False def test_delete_memory(tmp_path: Path): memory_file = tmp_path / "memory.json" item = add_memory("Test memory", memory_file) deleted = delete_memory(item.id, memory_file) assert deleted is True assert list_memory(memory_file) == [] def test_delete_missing_memory(tmp_path: Path): memory_file = tmp_path / "memory.json" deleted = delete_memory(999, memory_file) assert deleted is False def test_clear_memory(tmp_path: Path): memory_file = tmp_path / "memory.json" add_memory("Memory one", memory_file) clear_memory(memory_file) assert list_memory(memory_file) == [] def test_format_memory_for_display_empty(tmp_path: Path): memory_file = tmp_path / "memory.json" assert format_memory_for_display(memory_file) == "No saved memory." def test_format_memory_for_prompt(tmp_path: Path): memory_file = tmp_path / "memory.json" add_memory("I am learning Python.", memory_file) formatted = format_memory_for_prompt(memory_file) assert "I am learning Python." in formatted Test result: Python syntax check passed.

Create test_assistant.py:

7.18 How the Code Works

This project has four main parts.

Part 1: Command Parsing

The commands.py file turns user input into a command and content.

Example:

/remember I prefer concise explanations.

becomes:

command = "/remember" content = "I prefer concise explanations."

If the user types normal text without a command, it becomes /ask.

Part 2: Memory Store

The memory_store.py file saves memory to JSON.

It supports:

add_memory() list_memory() delete_memory() clear_memory()

Each memory has:

id text created_at

Part 3: Prompt with Memory Context

When the user asks a question, the app formats memory for the prompt.

memory_context = format_memory_for_prompt()

Then it builds a prompt:

Saved memory: - The user prefers concise explanations. Current user request: Explain RAG.

The model can use the memory if relevant.

Part 4: User Control

The user can inspect memory:

/memory

delete one item:

/forget 2

or clear everything:

/clear_memory

This is important.

Memory without user control is not trustworthy.

7.19 Sample User Session

A typical session may look like this:

Personal Study or Work Assistant with Memory ============================================================ Type /help to see commands. Type /remember to save user-approved memory. Type /exit to quit. ============================================================ You: /remember I prefer concise bullet-point explanations. Assistant: Saved memory 1: I prefer concise bullet-point explanations. You: /ask Explain RAG. Assistant: - RAG means Retrieval-Augmented Generation. - It lets an AI app retrieve relevant information before answering. - In Python, this often means searching documents, passing relevant chunks to an LLM, and generating an answer from that context. - It is useful for PDF chatbots, knowledge assistants, and support bots.

This is sample output only.

Do not claim exact output unless you run the code and capture the real result.

7.20 Testing the Project

Run:

pytest

Expected type of result:

21 passed

The exact number and timing may vary if you add more tests.

These tests check:

  • Memory creation
  • Memory deletion
  • Memory clearing
  • Secret detection
  • Command parsing
  • Assistant routing
  • Mock LLM use

The tests do not call the live model API.

That saves credits and keeps tests fast.

7.21 Live API Testing

After adding your API key to .env, run:

python app.py

Try:

/remember I am learning Python AI agents for freelancing.

Then ask:

/ask What project should I build next?

The assistant should use the saved memory if relevant.

Then inspect memory:

/memory

Then delete it:

/forget 1

Then check:

/memory

This tests the full memory cycle.

7.22 Memory and Privacy

Memory is useful, but privacy matters.

A memory assistant should not store secrets.

Bad memory:

My API key is sk-...

Good memory:

I prefer short explanations.

Bad memory:

My password is ...

Good memory:

I am studying for a Python interview.

The memory store in this chapter includes a basic secret detector.

It is not perfect.

It is a beginner safety layer.

For production systems, memory requires stronger security, user permissions, data retention rules, and privacy review.

7.23 Memory and Relevance

Not all memory is useful for every request.

Example memory:

The user prefers concise answers.

This is useful often.

Example request:

What is RAG?

The memory helps shape the answer.

But memory like:

The user is interested in freelancing.

may not matter when the user asks:

What is 2 + 2?

The prompt tells the model:

If saved memory is not relevant, ignore it.

This is important.

Too much irrelevant memory can make answers worse.

7.24 Memory vs RAG

Memory and RAG are related, but different.

FeatureMemoryRAG
StoresUser preferences or contextDocuments and knowledge
Example“User prefers short answers”PDF manual text
Used forPersonalizationGrounding answers
StorageJSON, database, vector DBVector database or search index
RiskPrivacyWrong retrieval or sensitive docs

In a strong assistant, you may use both.

Example:

Memory: The user is a beginner. RAG: Retrieved document chunk about embeddings. Answer: A beginner-friendly explanation using the retrieved chunk.

That is a powerful pattern.

7.25 Memory and Tools

Memory can also improve tool use.

Example memory:

The user prefers task lists with three priority levels.

When the user asks:

Create a task plan for building a PDF chatbot.

The assistant can format tasks as:

High priority Medium priority Low priority

Memory makes tools and workflows more personalized.

But tool actions should still be controlled by code and guardrails.

Do not let memory override safety rules.

7.26 Real-World Use Case

A memory assistant can support many practical workflows.

Study Assistant

Remember:

The user is preparing for Python interviews.

Then answer coding questions with interview tips.

Work Assistant

Remember:

The user prefers summaries with action items.

Then summarize meeting notes in that style.

Freelance Assistant

Remember:

The user specializes in AI automation for small businesses.

Then draft proposals with that positioning.

Writing Assistant

Remember:

The user prefers a clear, professional tone.

7.28 Common Mistakes

Mistake 1: Remembering Everything Automatically

Do not silently store every user message.

Use explicit memory commands.

Mistake 2: No Delete Option

Users should be able to delete memory.

Add /forget and /clear_memory.

Mistake 3: Storing Secrets

Never store API keys, passwords, or tokens.

Mistake 4: Using All Memory All the Time

Irrelevant memory can confuse the answer.

Tell the model to use memory only when relevant.

Mistake 5: Committing memory.json

Memory may contain user context.

Add it to .gitignore.

Mistake 6: Treating Local JSON as Production Storage

A JSON file is fine for learning.

Production apps need real databases, user isolation, and security review.

Mistake 7: Not Testing Memory Logic

Memory add, list, delete, and clear functions should be tested without the LLM.

7.29 Best Practices

Use explicit /remember.

Let users inspect memory.

Let users delete memory.

Let users clear all memory.

Block obvious secrets.

Store memory outside Git.

Use memory only when relevant.

Keep memory short.

Avoid sensitive data.

Test memory operations.

Document privacy limitations.
